Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

According to recent reports, “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”.

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

In a recent development, instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

According to recent reports, yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” indicates Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

It has been revealed that “I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a significant fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”.

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” claims the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, substantial mince dish.”.

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists.

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

In a recent development, haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

According to recent reports, from such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Sources indicate that bourdain, a native Newly introduced Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:.

But mark the Rustic, haggis-fed/.

The trembling earth resounds his tread/.

Clap in his ample fist a blade/.

And legs and arms and heads will cut/.

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, noted Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

According to recent reports, for Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

Best Mexican food: 23 dishes to try.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie noted.

In a recent development, “From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”.

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Sources indicate that such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he notes. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”.

Sonia Bompastor’s team had had by far the better of things at Plough Lane but created too little and were set to go into their final match in December needing favours from elsewhere, until in the 87th minute, Buurman found space at the near post to bundle a corner over the line.

Substitutes Lauren Hemp and Khadija Shaw struck to give Manchester City back-to-back wins in the Women’s Champions League with a 2-0 victory over Hacken in Gothenburg.

After three consecutive draws, City earned their second straight away European victory and boosted their chances of automatic qualification for the knockout phase.

Hemp and Shaw were introduced at the break and the former made the breakthrough 10 minutes after the interval after a defensive clearance ricocheted off her shin and into the net.

City thought they had doubled their lead shortly after through Mary Fowler, but it was ruled out for offside after Yui Hasegawa was stood in front of keeper Falk.

Hemp was then denied her second when she struck an effort off the post. But City were not to be denied, this time Hemp turned creator by giving it to an onrushing Shaw and she was able to tuck home in composed fashion.

City could have had a third but Falk guessed the right way to deny Fowler from the penalty spot after VAR adjudged Aivi Luik to have fouled Shaw inside the box.

Cambiaghi’s leveller in first-half added time came just three minutes after they had Karolina Lea Vilhjalmsdottir sent off, with an initial yellow card upgraded to red by VAR.

Inter defended resolutely after the break but their hearts were broken in the 85th minute when Bruun struck a rebound into an empty net. She sealed the win in stoppage time when she converted a penalty, which was awarded by VAR.

Juventus left it late to beat OH Leuven 2-0.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in.

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

Sources indicate that he’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.

Recent findings suggest that “We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”.

Sources indicate that it is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

Industry observers note that there was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

It has been revealed that pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

Industry observers note that all of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Recent findings suggest that athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

According to recent reports, pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”.

It has been revealed that eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach mentioned, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

Recent findings suggest that “The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very notable in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”.

Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Everton midfielder Leon Osman has praised David Moyes’ enduring legacy in the blue half of Merseyside, insisting the Scotsman’s Glaswegian grit made him the ideal fit the club.

Moyes transformed Everton’s fortunes during an 11-year spell on Merseyside between 2002 and 2013, consistently guiding the Toffees into the top half of the Premier League despite operating on a fraction of the transfer budgets enjoyed by their top-flight rivals.

While Moyes never lifted a major trophy during his tenure - falling just short in the 2009 FA Cup final against Chelsea - Osman believes his former boss’s ability to punch above his weight cements his status as one of the club’s most vital modern figures.

"For the majority of David Moyes' time in charge of Everton, he's probably overachieved in terms of what he's had to spend in the transfer market, so while he might not have had the success Harry Catterick did in terms of silverware, he's been so crucial for the club," Osman told Betway.

"He's a great fit for Everton, and I think it's that Glaswegian way that adapts particularly well to Liverpool because there's a real understanding of what the people of the city are like and what they want to see from their football team. Everton is the people's club first and foremost, and the fans want to see the team work hard and show that desire to be successful and that's something David Moyes has always instilled in his teams.".

In a recent development, osman was a central pillar of that Moyes era, making over 400 appearances for his boyhood club after breaking into the senior squad under the manager’s guidance. However, the former England international admitted he initially faced an uphill battle to prove he possessed the physicality required for top-flight football before becoming one of Moyes' most trusted lieutenants.

"He's the man who gave me my shot in the Premier League, so I'll always be thankful to him for that," Osman added. "It did take me a while, though, to convince him I was able and I was ready to play at that level, but once he gave me that chance I think he realised that we had very similar outlooks in terms of style of play and how the game should be played and we had a really great relationship throughout my career.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

According to recent reports, the right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that presently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

Sources indicate that the parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European Upcoming School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism.".

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl remarked.

According to recent reports, as anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has remarked that a latest proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

According to recent reports, "Words are worth nothing," the group remarked. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country.".

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media concern becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," stated Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM confirmed that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation.".

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

Latest Update: Record crowds, legends - Bordeaux bid to escape amateur game

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bordeaux fans protested when the club were demoted to the sixth tier.
  • The latest stop on Zinedine Zidane's homecoming tour was an important one for the new France head coach.
  • "I became a man in Bordeaux," Zidane fondly recalled in the build-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bordeaux fans protested when the club were demoted to the sixth tier.

The latest stop on Zinedine Zidane's homecoming tour was an important one for the new France head coach. When Les Bleus took on Turkey in Bordeaux on Sunday night, the ex-midfielder was returning to the city in which he spent four formative years of his playing career, between 1992 and 1996.

"I became a man in Bordeaux," Zidane fondly recalled in the build-up. France edged triumphed 2-1 with an uninspiring display, but it did not dampen the mood of the 40,000 fans inside the Stade Atlantique.

While the 1998 World Cup winner was not necessarily in familiar surroundings (the out-of-town stadium was built for Euro 2016, 20 years after his departure for Juventus), locals made every effort to make him feel at home, holding up a commemorative tifo before kick-off and chanting Zizou's name throughout.

Just a few miles up the road earlier that afternoon, Zidane's former club were playing their fifth match of the season in the sixth-tier Regional 1, in a north-western suburb of the city.

Thousands of Bordeaux fans had made the short away outing to Saint-Medard-en-Jalles' 3000-seater ground to watch their team seal a fifth win in five this season.

Girondins de Bordeaux, the six-time French champions, who were once regulars in European cups, now find themselves facing amateur opposition on a weekly basis.

Since 2022, the club has plummeted from Ligue 1 to the sixth tier through a combination of on-pitch struggles, mismanagement at all levels, and sanctions due to their financial troubles.

Listen to the latest Football Daily podcast.

The club was taken over in 2021 by Gerard Lopez, who was previously in charge of Formula 1's Lotus as well as another French side, Lille.

While Bordeaux were already hamstrung by debts at that point, the situation on and off the pitch worsened under the Spanish-Luxembourgish businessman as the men's first team finished rock bottom of Ligue 1 in his first season.

A couple of seasons in Ligue 2 followed, before the club was docked down to the fourth tier in 2024. In their first National 2 season, they notably signed Andy Carroll but ultimately missed out on promotion.

The following campaign saw a repeat of that near miss, and the club was expelled from national-level football altogether this summer over their finances.

With Bordeaux left on the brink and whittled down to just eight full-time employees (down from around 250 a few years beforehand), Lopez sold up to Park Bench, a group of mainly British USA-based investors who also own Scottish side Dunfermline as well as a minority stake in Spanish second tier side Cordoba.

The supporters turned out in their numbers for the first home match of the campaign, which had been delayed amid the uncertainty over whether the club could continue running, against Stade Montois.

More than 11,000 tickets sold, a record crowd for that level of French football.

"140 years of history, we won't be stopped," read one of the banners held up by the Ultramarines fan group, who also made it a point to thank the seven first-team players who had stayed despite the club's double relegation.

The team is centred around a core of players with Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 experience. Steve Shamal, who scored a hat-trick in that 4-1 victory over Stade Montois, previously turned out for the likes of Caen and Annecy in the second tier.

It has been revealed that "We know we should be higher up, but that certainty can also be a trap," stated Shamal after the game. "We shouldn't think that it's going to be easy.

"We need to respect our opponents if we're going to put in good performances.".

As the sixth tier of French football is regionalised, only the league winner in the Nouvelle Aquitaine region's top flight will earn promotion.

Industry observers note that their on-pitch success so far this season comes as little surprise given the gulf in quality compared to the rest of the league. Over the summer, Bordeaux notably managed to hold on to Europa League-winning full-back Almamy Toure, while former Belgian youth international striker Baptiste Guillaume also joined.

Several former players have also looked to get involved in Bordeaux's revival.

Benoit Tremoulinas, the former French international who was a part of the title-winning squad in 2008-09, notably revealed that at the age of 40 he would be lacing up his boots again seven years after injury forced him to retire.

Paul Baysse, the former centre-back, is an assistant to head coach Arnaud Cormier.

Benoit Tremoulinas spent six years at Bordeaux, winning a league title and two cups, before also twice winning the Europa League with Sevilla.

It has been revealed that perhaps the most significant endorsement the fresh owners could have hoped for was that of Alain Giresse, widely regarded as the club's greatest player. The Euro 1984 winner, who won three league titles while playing more than 500 times for the Marine et Blanc, was in attendance for the match against Stade Montois. He took the ceremonial kick-off before giving a full-time dressing room speech.

The upcoming management unveiled their long-term looks for the club on Monday at Le Haillan, the city-owned training ground which includes a chateau that hosts the club's headquarters.

"We are humbled to have this responsibility," Park Bench investor Jeremy Green stated.

"The club doesn't belong to Park Bench, it belongs to Bordeaux, it belongs to the 11,000 people who came to watch a Regional 1 game, to the players and to the community. We have a responsibility to rebuild this club.

"Our commitment to the community and to the players is that we will be fiscally responsible and patient.

"We're not a financial institution, we're a collection of individuals who bring with them business, sporting, analytical, and entrepreneurship skills.".

Dominique Delport, the club's new president, revealed he knew Green and Twining through his wife, who studied at Oxford with them.

"We can learn from the club's golden years," the former journalist and advertising executive told BBC Sport, before adding that he would look to bring club legends to every league game.

Bordeaux won the Coupe de France as recently as 2013.

While the club was sold for a symbolic euro, it did involve taking on long-standing debts which spanned transfer fees, stadium rent, and a compensation claim by former head coach Vladimir Petkovic.

Last Friday, the city's commercial court approved a request to restructure the debt as part of the club's continuation proposal.

When Bordeaux were expelled from national-level football by the French FA at the start of the summer, the club used several avenues to appeal while the takeover was being finalised.

"We thought we had acquired the club in National 1 [the fourth tier]," Green and co-investor James Twining, told BBC Sport.

In a recent development, "Initially we walked away, but we were encouraged to come back," Green added. "We established that we were going to be able to restructure things and make it work.

"People around the club and in the local community encouraged us to try to find a way.".

The six-time French champions have a long way to go before returning to the top flight.

"We're committing to a sensible financial structure, to a well-run club, and we're talking about 10 years to get this club back to Ligue 1," the fresh investors added.

A crucial step towards that long-term goal will be returning to the professional leagues, which would allow them to re-open the youth academy they were made to close when they dropped down.

Rebuilding the women's team, who were involved in the Champions League only a few seasons ago, is another one of the new owners' objectives.

Keeping the fans onside throughout the process will also be key, not least after the rift that opened up between groups during the previous ownership.

In any case, if the record-breaking turnout for Bordeaux's return to league action is anything to go by, their support seems unlikely to waver anytime soon.
